name: car_sedan
source: Geometry (wheelbase 2.70 m, track 1.56 m, wheel radius 0.317 m) matches data/models/car_sedan/car_sedan.rig.json. Mass (1500 kg curb weight) and a symmetric 50/50 front/rear static split are plausible round-number choices for a mid-size sedan (Genta, 'Motor Vehicle Dynamics', ch. 1 cites typical passenger-car curb weights of 1200-1700 kg and front/rear splits of roughly 50/50 to 60/40 - not a specific measured car). Suspension spring rates are chosen so the static-equilibrium compression sits at 1/3 of travel_max under this weight (see out/handover_p3.md's static-corner-weight note); damper rates target a ~0.35 damping ratio about that operating point via the usual 2*m*omega_n relation (Milliken, 'Race Car Vehicle Dynamics', ch. 16). All 4 wheels reference data/tyres/passenger_car_225_45r17.json. Placeholder drive torque curve (PLAN.md M1) is a plausible shape for a ~2.0 L naturally aspirated engine, not a specific published curve. final_drive_ratio=10.0 (out/handover_accel.md): DriveDesc has no separate gearbox/clutch stage (vehicle_desc.h's own header comment - 'no gearbox in this placeholder'), so this single ratio must stand in for a real car's launch (1st) gear times its differential, not the differential alone. The value originally here (3.7) was only a plausible standalone differential ratio (matching data/vehicles/tractor.json's own final_drive_ratio=15.0, which DOES already fold in the tractor's low working-gear reduction, for contrast) - with no gearbox multiplying it further, a stationary/idle-rpm launch only ever produced the torque curve's WEAKEST point (120 N*m at idle_rpm=900) times 3.7, giving a measured full-throttle standing-start acceleration of about 0.72 m/s^2 on asphalt (test_vehicle_accel_standing_start.cpp's diagnostic run), an order of magnitude below what this torque curve can deliver. 10.0 = a plausible 1st-gear ratio (~2.7, within the typical 2.9-3.8 range Genta ch. 6 cites for a 5/6-speed passenger-car gearbox's 1st gear, chosen at the low end here since it is multiplying an already-plausible 3.7 differential) times that same 3.7 differential ratio; a higher value (13.0, i.e. a 1st gear of ~3.5) was tried first and measured to push commanded wheel torque past the front tyres' peak Fx once engine rpm climbs off idle, producing a genuine (but undesired as this placeholder's baseline case) open-differential-style runaway wheelspin on one front wheel while the other stayed gripped - 10.0 stays torque-limited (not traction-limited) through the whole 0-50 km/h range, both front wheels tracking symmetrically, and measures ~3.2 m/s^2 average acceleration 0-50 km/h, matching a point-mass estimate from this same torque curve to within a few percent (test_vehicle_accel_standing_start.cpp). CAVEAT found while re-checking this fix against a live demo run: this 10.0 ratio is only low-slip/well-behaved when full throttle is commanded from an ALREADY-SETTLED rest (tyre contact/Fz established first, exactly test_vehicle_accel_standing_start.cpp's setup) - an INSTANTANEOUS full-throttle command issued before the suspension has settled (near-zero Fz, so near-zero tyre reaction torque) lets the wheel spin up essentially unopposed into deep post-peak slip, self-recovering over several seconds as the car's own speed catches up (never stalls, but runs at degraded Fx/Fz ~0.6 instead of ~1.0 during the excursion) - see vehicle_desc.h's DriveDesc comment and out/handover_accel.md for the full measured numbers and why this is treated as a documented placeholder (no clutch/traction-control) limitation rather than re-tuned away.
